title: Measure the human meaning your model leaves out.
dek: In the opening section of Chapter 6 of Alchemy, Rory Sutherland examines psychophysics: the gap between measurable physical change and the human experience of value.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: A small physical change can create a large perceptual shift. Before dismissing an effect as irrational, ask what the human experience is actually measuring.

canon.heading: Notice the value hidden inside the small change.
canon.standfirst: Read the opening section of Chapter 6, "Psychophysics," from Rory Sutherland's Alchemy on PDF pages 213-232. Study how perception turns modest physical differences into outsized changes in comfort, status, meaning, or choice.
canon.readerIntro: Read this section as a test of the distance between physical measurement and lived experience. Mark where Sutherland shows that people do not value inputs in a linear way, what perceptual threshold changes the meaning of an offer, and how context alters the felt value of an otherwise small difference. Then audit one product or service: name the physical change, the perceptual change it creates, and the decision it could unlock. Stop at PDF page 232.

blocks.label: 01 / Separate physical change from felt change
paragraphs: A measurable improvement is not automatically a meaningful improvement to a person.
Mark where the section distinguishes the physical input from the perceptual experience it produces.

blocks.label: 02 / Find the threshold
paragraphs: Psychophysics becomes commercially useful when a small change crosses a threshold of notice, comfort, status, or meaning.
Notice which cues make the difference legible enough to alter judgment.

blocks.label: 03 / Add the context
paragraphs: The same physical feature can feel valuable or pointless depending on the setting in which it is encountered.
Underline how context changes the value people assign to an apparently minor difference.

blocks.label: 04 / Audit one small change
paragraphs: Choose one product or service improvement that looks too small to matter in a purely technical specification.
Write the physical change, the perceptual shift it creates, and the buying or usage decision that shift could unlock.

closeReading: Where does Sutherland separate a physical improvement from the experience of improvement?
What threshold makes a small difference noticeable or meaningful?
How does context change the value a person assigns to the same feature?
Which example shows a perceptual shift doing more work than a larger technical change?
Choose one product or service: what small physical change could create a useful perceptual shift, and how would you test it?

principle.heading: Design for the experience the number cannot capture.
principle.body: A commercially important improvement may be small in physical terms but large in perception. Find the threshold where the change becomes felt, understood, and worth choosing.
principle.example: A hotel may spend less on a technically superior material and more on a small change in lighting, arrival, or tactile comfort that makes the room feel markedly more welcoming.
principle.practice: Pick one product or service and describe the smallest physical change that could produce the largest useful change in how it feels. Name the context and the behaviour you expect to change.

output.heading: Make the invisible value easier to feel.
output.body: The aim is not to ignore engineering or measurement. It is to notice where human perception multiplies, discounts, or redirects what the specification says should matter.

signals.heading: Four current signals about turning small perceptual shifts into value people can feel.

fieldNotes.title: Holiday brands are using human-made detail as a felt difference
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Marketing Dive reports that holiday marketers are balancing AI-enabled tactics with creator partnerships, deals, and human-made creative. Levi's used stop-motion claymation that required four hours of filming per second, while E.l.f. used stop-motion to make individuality tangible in its first holiday campaign.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The physical production difference is small relative to the media system around it, but it becomes a legible cue for care, craft, and distinctiveness. The perceptual shift is the point: viewers can feel that the work was made differently before they can explain why.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether the extra craft improves brand association and attention, or is remembered only as an executional novelty after the holiday campaign ends.

fieldNotes.title: Holiday shopping is stretching across more moments, not one sale day
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Retail Dive reports that consumers began shopping early to manage budgets, while nearly 30% plan to do most holiday shopping in early to mid-December, up from about 20% last year. BCG also finds generative AI becoming a tool of choice for finding and comparing products, with more than half of consumers using it in 2026.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The calendar is not just a schedule change; it changes the felt meaning of a promotion. Early discovery, comparison, and reassurance can matter as much as the discount itself because the shopper is managing uncertainty over time.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether retailers design different cues for early planning, comparison, and last-minute urgency, instead of repeating the same sale message across the whole season.

fieldNotes.title: Meta makes agentic help concrete through local connectors
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta made Muse available in Australia with local connectors across creativity, shopping, property, fitness, and entertainment, including Canva, Domain, Kogan, MECCA, Officeworks, and Ticketek. Users choose access and Muse checks with them before sensitive actions such as sending email or making a purchase.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The product becomes more understandable when an abstract agent is attached to familiar services and a visible permission boundary. The connector and approval details are small design choices, but they turn autonomy into something that can feel useful without feeling uncontrolled.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether local, everyday connectors create repeat behavior faster than a broad promise about an all-purpose personal agent.

fieldNotes.title: Google makes generated worlds easier to feel and revisit
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Google rolled out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie, adding real-time natural-language editing of environments, native audio, longer sessions, and a community gallery for sharing creations.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The new capability is easier to value because it crosses a perceptual threshold: generated worlds can now be changed, heard, and revisited as places rather than treated as one-off outputs. A gallery also makes the experience social and repeatable.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether longer sessions and sharing create a durable creative habit, or whether the novelty fades before Project Genie owns a clear job.

tweets.author: signüll
tweets.title: A product fragment about the feeling that numbers miss
tweets.summary: This fragment is useful because it tries to describe a product experience that the usual capability comparison cannot quite capture: the feeling of freshness, creative range, and ease of proposing ideas.
tweets.text:
i'm admittedly pretty harsh on the google guys, mostly cuz i know the co super well.

but holy hell, i'm having an incredible time with neon so far.

product issues aside, this is a very different experience, almost like a strange new feeling. the way it talks, the way it responds, everything feels pretty damn fresh if that makes any sense. it's very creative. & unusually great at proposing ideas. i am normally okay with words, but this is very difficult for me to articulate well.

anyway, it's fairly clear that google absolutely cooked here.

i have never doubted google's technical capabilities. those were & are totally obvious. i mean it is literally the birth place of ai. it was always a question of whether google could turn an extraordinary technology into newer experiences that ppl love using, which sort of requires shedding every success of the past.

these newer generation of models, particularly neon clearly gives them extraordinary new legs to stand on. it doesn't feel like "gemini" at all.

congratulations to everyone at google, i will continue to play around with more. there are obviously some product frustrations & confusing elements but i'm setting those aside for now.

signals.tweetHeading: One fragment from the timeline worth carrying into the work.
